message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This bid is unusual in that it is not based on assumptions about demand: we tested the exact opening pattern at Ashgrove before asking for a penny, and measured the results hour by hour. The pilot showed strong uptake, with evening visits running close to daytime levels and Sunday sessions very popular with families, and new memberships up by about two-thirds on the year before. That gives Members real local evidence that the hours will be used. The costing is equally careful. Staffing is built up from first principles, hours times staff times weeks times branches at the correct graded rate with on-costs, and utilities are taken from actual pilot spend rather than estimates, all of which sums to £174,000. We also looked seriously at the cheaper self-service alternative and explain why it would cost more once building works are included. I am confident this is a well-tested, carefully costed proposal that delivers on the Council Plan.
</author>

<document>
Budget Justification: Extended Opening Hours at Five Branch Libraries, 2027-28
Library Services, Westmoor Borough Council, September 2026

1. Request
Library Services requests a growth bid of £174,000 in the 2027-28 revenue budget to extend opening hours at five branch libraries (Ashgrove, Fenwick, Holt Lane, Kingsmead and Millbrook) by ten hours a week each, from 38 to 48 hours.

2. Rationale
The five branches currently close at 5 pm on weekdays and do not open on Sundays. Residents' surveys have repeatedly identified opening hours as the main barrier to library use among working-age adults: in the 2025 Residents' Survey, 44% of non-users aged 25-54 said the library "is never open when I can go". The Council Plan commits to increasing library use among working-age residents and to supporting adult learning and job-seeking.

Each branch would add late opening until 8 pm on Tuesdays and Thursdays (six additional hours) and Sunday opening from 11 am to 3 pm (four additional hours).

3. Evidence from the Ashgrove pilot
From October 2025 to March 2026, Ashgrove trialled exactly this pattern, funded from one-off underspends.

Table 1. Ashgrove pilot: average visits per opening hour, October 2025 to March 2026
Time slot | Visits per hour
Weekday 9 am - 12 pm | 46
Weekday 12 pm - 5 pm | 58
Tuesday and Thursday 5 pm - 8 pm (new) | 21
Saturday 9 am - 1 pm | 64
Sunday 11 am - 3 pm (new) | 52

Over the pilot, Ashgrove recorded 1,140 new library memberships, compared with 690 in the same months a year earlier. Sunday sessions were particularly popular with families, and a weekly job club in the Thursday evening slot was fully booked from its third week.

Evening visits at Ashgrove averaged close to the weekday daytime level, which shows that there is strong latent demand for evening opening and that the new hours will be well used across all five branches.

4. Costs
Additional hours need two staff on duty at all times, in line with the Council's lone-working policy. Staffing is calculated on 50 weeks a year, allowing for bank holiday closures.

Table 2. Cost of extended hours, five branches
Item | Basis | Cost
Staffing | 10 hours x 2 staff x 50 weeks x 5 branches = 5,000 hours at £24.80 per hour (including on-costs) | £124,000
Utilities and caretaking | £6,500 per branch | £32,500
Self-service kiosk upgrades (maintenance contract) | 5 branches | £7,500
Total | | £174,000

The staffing rate is the mid-point of the Library Assistant grade plus 28% on-costs and an enhancement for Sunday working. Utilities and caretaking costs are based on the actual additional costs recorded at Ashgrove during the pilot, scaled to a full year.

5. Value for money
At current visit rates, the extra hours across the five branches would generate roughly 84,000 additional visits a year, at a cost of around £2 per visit. This compares favourably with the borough's average cost per library visit of £3.40.

6. Alternatives considered
We considered opening the branches with self-service access only in the extra hours, as some authorities have done. This would cut staffing costs by around two-thirds, but the Council's insurers have advised that unstaffed opening would require building alterations and CCTV at an estimated £60,000 per branch, and it would not support the job club and family activities that drove much of the pilot's success.

7. Risks
Recruitment. We expect to fill most additional hours from existing part-time staff who have asked for more hours, as happened during the pilot.
Demand at other branches. Ashgrove is our busiest branch, and demand at the other four may be lower. We will review usage after six months.

8. Conclusion
The twelve-month Ashgrove pilot has demonstrated strong demand for evening and Sunday opening, with new memberships up by two-thirds and evening use close to daytime levels. We ask Members to approve a growth bid of £174,000 to extend this successful model to all five branches from April 2027.
</document>
response:
The case for extending hours is reasonable, and the Sunday evidence is genuinely strong. But the bid is £10,000 higher than its own cost lines add up to. Evening use was well under half of daytime use, not "close" to it. The visit and value-for-money figures assume every branch performs like Ashgrove, the busiest. The bid also describes a six-month pilot as twelve months.

## What holds up

- **Staffing:** 10 × 2 × 50 × 5 = 5,000 hours, and at £24.80 an hour that is £124,000 ✓
- **Utilities:** £6,500 × 5 = £32,500 ✓
- **Memberships:** 1,140 against 690 is +65%, which matches "about two-thirds" ✓
- **Additional visits:** 6 evening hours × 21 plus 4 Sunday hours × 52 gives 334 a week. Over 50 weeks and 5 branches that is about 84,000 ✓ as arithmetic
- **Sunday demand:** 52 visits an hour is close to weekday daytime levels (46–58), and the job club filled up. That is real evidence of demand.

## Main problems

**1. The cost lines add up to £164,000, not £174,000.** £124,000 + £32,500 + £7,500 = **£164,000**. Either a £10,000 line is missing or the total is wrong. As it stands, Members would approve £10,000 more than the costing supports.

**2. Evening use was well under half of daytime use.** Evenings averaged 21 visits an hour, against 46–58 on weekday daytimes. That is **36–46% of daytime use**, not "close to" it. The bid's statements that evening use shows "strong latent demand" and was "close to daytime levels" are contradicted by Table 1.

The difference matters for value for money. Spreading the costs evenly across the 2,500 extra branch-hours gives:

| Cost per extra branch-hour | £ |
|---|---|
| Staffing (£124,000 / 2,500) | 49.60 |
| Utilities and caretaking | 13.00 |
| Kiosk maintenance | 3.00 |
| **Total** | **≈ 65.60** |

| Slot at Ashgrove | Visits per hour | Cost per visit |
|---|---|---|
| Sunday | 52 | **≈ £1.26** |
| Tuesday and Thursday evening | 21 | **≈ £3.12** |

At Ashgrove, Sunday opening is excellent value, and evening opening is far less clearly so. At the other four branches, which Section 7 says may be quieter, evening visits could easily cost more than the borough average.

**3. The visit forecast applies Ashgrove's figures to all five branches.** Section 7 says Ashgrove is the busiest branch and the others may be quieter, yet Section 5 uses Ashgrove's rates for all five. The forecast also counts every visit in the new hours as additional. Some of those visitors would have come during existing hours anyway. The pilot data could test this by checking whether Ashgrove's daytime visits fell. On both counts, 84,000 is an upper estimate.

**4. The value-for-money comparison doesn't compare like with like.** Roughly £2 per visit is the extra cost of the new hours only. The £3.40 borough figure is an average across all running costs: buildings, stock, management and so on. Extra hours will almost always look cheaper than that average. A fairer comparison sets the £2 against the extra cost per visit of other options, or uses the slot-level figures above.

**5. The pilot ran for six months, not twelve.** October 2025 to March 2026 is six months, but the Conclusion calls it "the twelve-month Ashgrove pilot".

## Smaller points

- **Memberships.** The 65% rise isn't shown to be caused by the new hours. What happened to memberships at the other branches over the same months?
- **Self-service alternative.** Section 6 doesn't actually show self-service would cost more, despite the author's description. It would save about £83,000 a year in staffing against £300,000 of one-off building works, so it pays back in under four years. The stronger argument against it is the one the bid already makes: unstaffed hours can't support the job club or family activities. A hybrid is worth considering, with staff on Sundays and Thursday evenings (for the job club) and self-service or no opening on Tuesday evenings.
- **Utilities.** Scaling winter costs (October–March) up to a full year probably overstates heating and lighting. That error leans towards caution, which is fine, but the bid should say so.
- **Staffing rate.** The bid should say whether £24.80 is a blended rate covering the Sunday enhancement across all hours, and whether it covers holiday cover for the extra hours.
- **Kiosk line.** The kiosk line is labelled "upgrades" but costed as a maintenance contract. It should be described consistently.

## On the author's description

- **"Tested the exact pattern" and "measured hour by hour".** Accurate, and the pilot is the bid's real strength.
- **"Evening visits running close to daytime levels".** Evening visits were 21 an hour against 46–58 in the daytime.
- **"Sums to £174,000".** The lines sum to £164,000.
- **"Self-service would cost more once building works are included".** Over any period beyond about four years, it would cost less. The stronger reason to reject it is the loss of staffed activities.

## Suggested changes before Members decide

1. Correct the total to £164,000, or identify the missing £10,000.
2. Describe evening demand accurately, and show cost per visit by slot.
3. Forecast visits with a lower assumption for the four other branches, and check whether daytime visits fell during the pilot.
4. Change "twelve-month" to "six-month".
5. Consider funding Sundays at all five branches and evenings selectively, starting with Thursday for the job club. Then review after six months as already planned.

The Sunday case is strong enough to stand on its own. The evening case needs to be argued on its actual numbers.
